program_meta.program_name: PhD in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), MIT School of Engineering / MIT Schwarzman College of Computing. CSAIL, LIDS, IDSS, RLE and IMES are laboratories, not degree-granting units - you apply to EECS (or to IDSS / HST as alternate pools for some PIs) and then join a lab.
program_meta.sop_limit: not stated on any public MIT EECS page. EECS does NOT ask for a single 'statement of purpose'; the FAQ states the application consists of 'the biographical section, three (3) letters of recommendation, "Record of Subjects" with grades, and two essays, one about your Research Activities and Goals, and the other about your Academic and Intellectual Journey.' No word or page cap for either essay is published on the admission-process page or the Graduate Admissions FAQs; the caps appear only inside the GradApply portal (opens ~15 September). The MIT EECS Communication Lab CommKit says only that applicants should 'adhere to the length and formatting guidelines of the program to which you are applying (usually no more than 2 pages)' - that is generic advice, NOT an EECS rule. VERIFY inside gradapply.mit.edu/eecs once the Fall 2027 form opens.
program_meta.extra_essays: Yes - a second required essay, 'Academic and Intellectual Journey', in addition to 'Research Activities and Goals'. Limits not stated publicly. Note the FAQ says 'A few sections of the application are editable after submission, including the "Research Activities and Goals" and "Academic and Intellectual Journey" essays.' Supplementary material is explicitly discouraged: 'Because of the large volume of applications submitted to EECS, we must discourage you from sending in copies of awards, journal articles, and other extraneous documents. You may provide URLs to these documents in your application in the "Honors, Prizes, Awards, and Fellowships" box.'
program_meta.deadline_fall_2027: Not yet published as of 2026-08-28. The most recently posted cycle (entry September 2026) states: application website 'available on September 15, 2025' and 'The deadline for submitting completed applications is December 1, 2025.' MIT EECS has used a fixed 1 December deadline, so Fall 2027 entry is expected to open ~15 September 2026 and close ~1 December 2026 - treat as UNCONFIRMED and re-check eecs.mit.edu in September 2026. FAQ note: 'the deadline for submitting your application is December 1 and the online application system will shut down that day. However, the online letter system will stay open for several more weeks.'
program_meta.lor_count: Three (3), uploaded electronically by recommenders to GradApply. Employer/supervisor letters are acceptable where faculty letters are hard to obtain.
program_meta.gre: Not required and not used. FAQ verbatim: 'We do not use the GRE test scores during the admission process - regardless of citizenship - unless you are applying to the LGO Program, which does require the GRE.'
program_meta.english_test: TOEFL, IELTS or Duolingo accepted. EECS minimums: TOEFL iBT 100 (600 paper-based, 250 computer-based); IELTS 7.0; Duolingo 130. ETS code for MIT is 3514, EECS department code 66 (or 78). INDIA-RELEVANT EXEMPTION: the waiver is automatic if 'The student has earned a degree from an accredited institution where English is the main language of instruction' and, verbatim, 'In the case of institutions not located in the US / other English-speaking nations, so long as it is stated on your transcript that the language of instruction was English, then the transcript itself would fulfill the requirement for a waiver.' => Akshat should check whether the MIT Bengaluru / MAHE transcript explicitly states English as the medium of instruction; if it does, no TOEFL/IELTS is needed.
program_meta.app_fee: USD $90, paid by credit card. Fee waivers are handled by the MIT Office of Graduate Education via the 'OGE Fee Waiver Request Form for EECS'. FAQ warning: 'Emails to grad-ap@eecs.mit.edu asking for an application fee waiver do not constitute a formal request using the OGE form and will not be reviewed.'
program_meta.faculty_directory_url: https://eecsis.mit.edu/research_interests.pcgi (EECS Faculty Interests Guide, linked from the official admission-process page); https://www.csail.mit.edu/people?person%5B0%5D=role%3A299 (CSAIL Principal Investigators); https://www.eecs.mit.edu/research/artificial-intelligence-decision-making/
program_meta.advisor_model: Admitted to the DEPARTMENT, not to an individual advisor - but faculty interest matters heavily. FAQ: 'Research assistants are chosen by faculty who are seeking students who share their research interests' and 'Once a student has been admitted, some interviews and student visits will be arranged in order to determine the level of shared interest between the student and faculty.' Applicants tag/name faculty in the GradApply system (Kaiming He: 'submit your application to the EECS admission process ... and tag my name in the system'). Marzyeh Ghassemi's lab states verbatim: 'Unfortunately, MIT does not allow for direct admission from an individual PI to the institution.' Funding is guaranteed via fellowship, RA or TA: 'The financial support provides full tuition, a monthly living stipend and medical insurance.' Some PIs also draw from IDSS, HST, MIT-WHOI, EAPS or CEE pools.
program_meta.ms_research_access: Not applicable for external applicants - there is NO terminal master's. Verbatim from the admission-process page: 'Application is for the doctoral program only - there is no terminal masters degree, but all PhD students earn a masters degree as they work towards PhD. A Masters of Engineering is only available for qualified MIT EECS undergraduates.' FAQ: 'When we admit an applicant, it is into the PhD program. If you do not have a master's degree when you apply, you will get that degree first before proceeding to the PhD.' EECS also does not accept transfer credit from another university's started MS/PhD.
program_meta.notes: Only one admissions process exists for MS and PhD. Applicants who already hold a PhD are not admitted. Decisions are released through the separate 'MIT Application Management' system (two accounts are needed: GradApply + MIT Application Management). Departmental contact for admissions questions: grad-ap@eecs.mit.edu; platform questions: gradadmissions@mit.edu. Akshat should apply to EECS as his primary pool; Ghassemi (IDSS/HST) and Beery (MIT-WHOI/EAPS/CEE) accept alternate pools if EECS is a stretch.

faculty.rank: Associate Professor with tenure, EECS (also part-time Distinguished Scientist, Google DeepMind)
faculty.research_areas: Self-supervised representation learning (MoCo, MAE), denoising/diffusion generative models, one-step and flow-map generative modelling, dataset bias, controlled 'deconstruction' studies of what makes representations work.
faculty.why_match: Akshat's DDPM-pretraining study on unlabelled BTCV abdominal CT found liver Dice rise 0.751 -> 0.928 with a frozen encoder retaining 87% of the fine-tuned liver Dice, while the SAME frozen encoder fell BELOW random initialisation on kidney - i.e. a diffusion pretext task confers transferable structure for some anatomy and not others, and he could not say which component of the diffusion objective did the work. He's 'Deconstructing Denoising Diffusion Models for Self-Supervised Learning' (ICLR 2025) is precisely that experiment run at scale: strip a DDPM down component by component until you isolate what actually produces good representations. His 'A Decade's Battle on Dataset Bias: Are We There Yet?' (ICLR 2025 Oral) is the same rigorous-empiricist genre Akshat works in - a controlled test of an assumption everyone had stopped checking.
faculty.key_paper_1: Deconstructing Denoising Diffusion Models for Self-Supervised Learning. Xinlei Chen, Zhuang Liu, Saining Xie, Kaiming He. ICLR 2025 (tech report Jan 2024).
faculty.key_paper_2: A Decade's Battle on Dataset Bias: Are We There Yet? Zhuang Liu, Kaiming He. ICLR 2025 (Oral).
faculty.taking_students: Yes - homepage (retrieved 2026-08-28) carries an active prospective-PhD instruction for the upcoming cycle.
faculty.contact_policy: VERBATIM: 'Prospective PhD students: if you are interested in joining my group as a PhD, please submit your application to the EECS admission process (opening Sept.) and tag my name in the system.' And: 'Prospective interns and post-docs: if you are interested in joining my group, please email me with your CV and a short research statement.' => Email is invited ONLY for interns/postdocs; PhD applicants are directed to the application system, not to email.
faculty.email_angle: Do not cold-email as a PhD applicant - his page routes PhD interest to the application. Instead, in the EECS essay: 'Deconstructing Denoising Diffusion Models asked which part of a DDPM makes the representation; my BTCV experiment ran into the flip side - the same diffusion-pretrained frozen encoder kept 87% of fine-tuned liver Dice but fell below random init on kidney, and I could not say why.'
faculty.notes: Still at MIT (joined 2024, tenured Associate Professor). Holds a concurrent PART-TIME Distinguished Scientist role at Google DeepMind, stated on his own page - not a departure, but worth knowing. His group is now heavily generative-modelling-focused (Mean Flows, Fractal Generative Models, Bidirectional Normalizing Flow); medical imaging is NOT a topic in his group, so pitch the methodological question, not the application. Extremely competitive.

faculty.rank: Sunlin (1966) and Priscilla Chou Professor of EECS
faculty.research_areas: Biomedical image analysis; segmentation and registration under scarce annotation; statistical/shape modelling of anatomy; learning general-purpose biomedical volume representations from randomized synthesis; fetal and clinical neuroimaging.
faculty.why_match: Akshat's SPIDER lumbar-spine work trained a teacher on only 54 labelled MRI slices (0.735 mIoU), filtered its pseudo-labels by confidence, and lifted a student to 0.816 mIoU (+8.1 points) - and showed the per-class thresholds calibrated on just 5 reference images matched those calibrated on 304, i.e. the calibration set can be tiny. Golland's 'Learning General-purpose Biomedical Volume Representations using Randomized Synthesis' (ICLR 2025, senior author with Dalca) attacks the same annotation bottleneck from the opposite direction - build the supervision synthetically so you need almost no real labels - and her 'AnyStar' (WACV 2024) does domain-randomised 3D instance segmentation with no real annotated training data. Akshat's negative result (combining MC-dropout uncertainty with confidence thresholding adds nothing) is exactly the kind of calibration question her group works on.
faculty.key_paper_1: Learning General-purpose Biomedical Volume Representations using Randomized Synthesis. N. Dey, B. Billot, H.E. Wong, C.J. Wang, M. Ren, P.E. Grant, A.V. Dalca, P. Golland. ICLR 2025.
faculty.key_paper_2: AnyStar: Domain randomized universal star-convex 3D instance segmentation. N. Dey, S.M. Abulnaga, B. Billot, E.A. Turk, P.E. Grant, A.V. Dalca, P. Golland. WACV 2024.
faculty.taking_students: Yes for MIT PhD students only. Homepage (last updated 06 Nov 2025): 'I do not have visiting or research assistant positions in my group and only work with MIT PhD students. To join the group, please apply to the EECS PhD program.'
faculty.contact_policy: VERBATIM: 'I do not have visiting or research assistant positions in my group and only work with MIT PhD students. To join the group, please apply to the EECS PhD program. I will be happy to discuss potential projects and areas of interest once you are admitted. I cannot answer emails with inquiries about visiting positions, internships and admissions, please inquire directly with the department.' => DO NOT EMAIL HER about admissions. This is an explicit no-email policy.
faculty.email_angle: No email. Name her in the 'Research Activities and Goals' essay: 'AnyStar removes the need for real annotations by randomising the generator; my SPIDER study kept the annotations but shrank them to 54, and found the confidence thresholds that make pseudo-labels usable can be calibrated on 5 images.'
faculty.notes: Currently at MIT; CSAIL profile and personal page both active (personal page updated Nov 2025). She is the single best-aligned senior MIT person for interests A + E. Her explicit no-email-about-admissions rule is the strongest contact constraint in this file - respect it.

faculty.rank: Assistant Professor (HMS / MGH), with MIT EECS appointment; Director, Computational Core, A.A. Martinos Center for Biomedical Imaging
faculty.department: Harvard Medical School / Massachusetts General Hospital AND MIT EECS (his group page lists him as 'Assistant Professor, HMS, MGH & MIT EECS')
faculty.lab: Dalca group at the Martinos Center, spanning MGB / HMS / MIT CSAIL; several students co-mentored with John Guttag (MIT) and Bruce Fischl (Harvard)
faculty.research_areas: Label-efficient and general-purpose medical image segmentation (in-context learning, prompting); robust learning through procedural/synthetic data generation (SynthSeg, SynthMorph, SynthStrip, Anatomix); learning-based registration (VoxelMorph); hypernetworks and amortised hyperparameter learning.
faculty.why_match: Two of Akshat's results sit directly inside this group's agenda. (1) A-PDF generates cWGAN-GP augmentations and then FILTERS them post hoc by scoring each synthetic mask against the class-proportion distribution of 447 real masks (Mahalanobis retains 33.7%, kNN 35.1%) rather than trusting the discriminator - a quality-control layer on synthetic data, which is exactly the gap in Dalca's procedural-synthesis line (SynthSeg/Anatomix generate aggressively but do not score what they generate). (2) Akshat's polyp study held architecture fixed and measured what preprocessing alone contributes across three backbones (+0.0226 to +0.0579 Dice), finding the gain SHRINKS as the architecture strengthens. Dalca's 'UniverSeg: Universal Medical Image Segmentation' (ICCV 2023) and 'Tyche: Stochastic In-Context Learning for Medical Image Segmentation' (CVPR 2024) push in the same direction - make one model handle a new task from a tiny support set instead of retraining an architecture per task.
faculty.key_paper_1: UniverSeg: Universal Medical Image Segmentation. V.I. Butoi*, J.J.G. Ortiz*, T. Ma, M.R. Sabuncu, J. Guttag, A.V. Dalca. ICCV 2023, pp. 21381-21394.
faculty.key_paper_2: Tyche: Stochastic In-Context Learning for Medical Image Segmentation. M. Rakic, H.E. Wong, J.J.G. Ortiz, B. Cimini, J. Guttag, A.V. Dalca. CVPR 2024 (Highlight, 2.8% of submissions).
faculty.taking_students: Unstated on his site. Evidence he currently advises MIT EECS PhD students: his group page (retrieved 2026-08-28) lists Marianne Rakic, Hallee Wong, Andrew Hoopes, Victor Butoi and Catherine Gai all as 'PhD Student, MIT EECS'. Publication record through 2026 is active (ICLR 2026, NeurIPS 2025).
faculty.contact_policy: not stated - no prospective-student or no-email instruction appears anywhere on adalca.mit.edu (home, group or publications pages). His homepage does state: 'I am open to selected advisory roles, industry collaborations, and conversations around startups or research spinouts' - that is about industry, not students.
faculty.email_angle: A short, specific email is defensible here since no policy forbids it: 'UniverSeg and Tyche make one model adapt to a new segmentation task from a tiny support set. I built the complementary piece by accident - a post-hoc filter that scores cWGAN-GP-generated masks against the class-proportion distribution of 447 real ones, keeping ~34%, because the discriminator's own score was not a usable quality signal.'
faculty.notes: IMPORTANT STRUCTURAL CAVEAT: his primary faculty appointment is Harvard Medical School / MGH (Martinos Center), with an MIT EECS affiliation. He clearly does advise MIT EECS PhD students, but he is not listed as an EECS core faculty member with an independent MIT admissions slot - an EECS application naming him may need a co-advisor (historically John Guttag). Also note he is actively exploring industry advisory roles and spinouts; that is disclosed on his own page and is not a departure, but it signals divided attention.

faculty.rank: Assistant Professor; Homer A. Burnell Career Development Professor
faculty.department: MIT EECS (Faculty of AI and Decision Making)
faculty.lab: Beery Lab, CSAIL; co-PI, NSF/NSERC Global Center on AI and Biodiversity Change
faculty.research_areas: Computer vision for biodiversity and environmental monitoring under real-world data pathologies: domain shift, imperfect/noisy labels, fine-grained and taxonomic categories, long-tailed distributions, active learning, synthetic data for rare classes, benchmark integrity.
faculty.why_match: Akshat's CVIP 2025 paper is a controlled benchmark of U-Net, ResU-Net, Attention U-Net and U-Net++ for lung segmentation whose finding is a negative one - no variant is universally best. Beery's 'Align and Distill: Unifying and Improving Domain Adaptive Object Detection' (TMLR 2025, Featured) is the same methodological intervention on a whole subfield: it shows published domain-adaptive detection comparisons were confounded by unequal implementations and re-runs them fairly. Her 'Synthetic Examples Improve Generalization for Rare Classes' (WACV 2020) is the ancestor of Akshat's A-PDF, and her 'A Deep Active Learning System for Species Identification and Counting in Camera Trap Images' (Methods in Ecology and Evolution 2021) is the label-efficiency loop his SPIDER pseudo-labelling pipeline reinvents in a medical setting. Her taxonomic fine-grained species work is also the closest MIT analogue to HiME's 4-level Galaxy Zoo 2 hierarchy.
faculty.key_paper_1: Align and Distill: Unifying and Improving Domain Adaptive Object Detection. J. Kay, T. Haucke, S. Stathatos, S. Deng, E. Young, P. Perona, S. Beery, G. Van Horn. TMLR 2025 (Featured).
faculty.key_paper_2: A Deep Active Learning System for Species Identification and Counting in Camera Trap Images. M.S. Norouzzadeh, D. Morris, S. Beery, N. Joshi, N. Jojic, J. Clune. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 2021.
faculty.taking_students: Yes, via application only. Homepage: 'I consider students primarily via MIT EECS and the MIT-WHOI joint program, but I would be open to advising students with the right fit for my lab through MIT EAPS or MIT CEE if that is better aligned with your background ... apply to any of these programs and list me in your application.'
faculty.contact_policy: VERBATIM: 'If you are interested in any position with the group (Postdoc, PhD, MEng, UROP, Visitor), instead of emailing me please fill out the interest survey below so I can better organize my responses. I am unlikely to respond to individual emails.' And: 'Unfortunately I am unlikely to be able to meet with prospective applicants before they have gone through the formal review process.' Interest survey: https://forms.gle/WkofxoM4q5upNtSn8
faculty.email: beery@mit.edu (also listed as beery@csail.mit.edu on the CSAIL directory)
faculty.email_angle: Do NOT email - use her interest survey. Survey/essay hook: 'Align and Distill showed a whole subfield's comparisons were confounded; my U-Net-variant benchmark for lung segmentation reached the same uncomfortable place on a smaller scale - once the training pipeline is held fixed, no variant is universally best.'
faculty.notes: Currently at MIT (was previously a visiting researcher at Google - that is historical, she is now MIT EECS faculty with an NSF CAREER and AI2050 fellowship). Domain is ecology/conservation, NOT medicine - so this is a method match, not a domain match, and the essay must be honest about that. She explicitly will not meet applicants pre-review, so the application itself has to carry the argument.

faculty.lab: Atomic Architects; MIT Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE)
faculty.research_areas: Equivariant and geometric deep learning (e3nn, tensor field networks) - symmetry constraints satisfied by construction rather than learned; representation and abstraction: what should be made explicit vs. left implicit, and how representations relate information across levels of description.
faculty.why_match: HiME composes per-level conditional sigmoids by the chain rule so a child's probability can never exceed its parent's, which makes the prediction set upward-closed at ANY threshold - hierarchy consistency is a theorem, not a post-hoc repair, and it survived across ViT-B/16, ViT-L/16, ResNet-50, ConvNeXt-T and EfficientNet-B0 at ~0.01% parameter overhead on Galaxy Zoo 2 (239,573 images, 37 classes, 4 levels). That is structurally the same move as Smidt's 'Tensor field networks': build the invariance into the operator so it holds exactly, rather than training the network to approximate it. Her posted Fall 2027 note asks 'What should be made explicit or left implicit? How should representations relate information across different scales or levels of description?' - which is almost verbatim Akshat's own unifying question (build structure in vs. let the model learn it from data).
faculty.key_paper_1: Tensor field networks: Rotation- and translation-equivariant neural networks for 3D point clouds. N. Thomas, T. Smidt, S. Kearnes, L. Yang, L. Li, K. Kohlhoff, P. Riley. arXiv:1802.08219 (basis of the e3nn framework, linked from her own Code and Papers page).
faculty.key_paper_2: A Recipe for Charge Density Prediction. X. Fu, A. Rosen, K. Bystrom, R. Wang, A. Musaelian, B. Kozinsky, T. Smidt, T. Jaakkola. NeurIPS 2024.
faculty.taking_students: Barely. She has a dedicated page 'Prospective Fall 2027 PhD Students' (the exact cycle Akshat is applying to) stating she expects at most one student and may take none.
faculty.contact_policy: VERBATIM from https://blondegeek.github.io/prospective : 'I expect to take at most one new PhD student this admissions cycle, and may not take any.' ... 'I am not currently looking specifically to grow the group in equivariant or atomistic machine learning.' ... 'For the small number of students I might consider taking this year, I care less about alignment with a particular existing research program than about a shared intellectual interest in these questions and the possibility of discovering something interesting together.' No explicit instruction about email either way - so 'not stated' on emailing, but the capacity warning is unambiguous. She also states on her homepage: 'Late 2026 - early 2027: Taking a break from speaking and professional travel surrounding maternity leave.'
faculty.email_angle: If contacting at all, lead with her stated question, not her published area: 'Your Fall 2027 note asks what should be made explicit vs. left implicit. In HiME I made a 4-level taxonomy explicit in the decoding rule - chain-rule composition of conditional sigmoids - so hierarchy consistency holds by construction; the uncomfortable finding was that the same constraint costs accuracy under a frozen encoder (0.858) and is free under a fine-tuned one (0.952).'
faculty.notes: Currently at MIT EECS (Associate Professor; also RLE). Rated Partial rather than Close ONLY because her published record is equivariant/atomistic ML for physical systems, a different domain from Akshat's - the method-level overlap (guarantees by construction) is genuinely strong. TWO RED FLAGS: (a) at most one student, possibly zero, for exactly this cycle; (b) maternity leave late 2026 - early 2027, overlapping the review period. Do not make her the sole named PI in the MIT essay.

faculty.lab: Isola lab, CSAIL (part of the Embodied Intelligence and Visual Computing communities)
faculty.research_areas: Representation learning; representational universals across models and modalities (Platonic Representation Hypothesis); what pretraining on synthetic/procedural data actually confers; self-supervised and generative representation learning; emergent intelligence.
faculty.why_match: Akshat's diffusion-pretraining result splits cleanly along a line Isola's group studies: the frozen DDPM encoder retained 87% of the fine-tuned liver Dice but scored 0.654 on kidney against a 0.899 random-init baseline - so the pretext task transferred perception of one structure and not another, with no principled account of why. Isola's 'Separating Knowledge and Perception with Procedural Data' (ICML 2025) is exactly this decomposition: it asks which part of what a pretrained model 'knows' is perceptual and reconstructible from procedural/synthetic data versus genuinely knowledge-bearing. His 'Personalized Representation from Personalized Generation' (ICML 2025, with Beery) is also directly relevant to A-PDF's use of generated images to improve a downstream representation.
faculty.key_paper_1: Separating Knowledge and Perception with Procedural Data. A. Rodriguez-Munoz, M. Baradad, P. Isola, A. Torralba. ICML 2025.
faculty.key_paper_2: Personalized Representation from Personalized Generation. S. Sundaram*, J. Chae*, Y. Tian, S. Beery, P. Isola. ICML 2025.
faculty.taking_students: Unstated. No admissions statement on his homepage as of 2026-08-28; group is large and actively publishing (10 listed PhD students, papers through 2026).
faculty.contact_policy: not stated - no prospective-student or no-email instruction found on web.mit.edu/phillipi as of 2026-08-28.
faculty.email: phillipi@mit.edu (listed on his homepage in spaced-out form: 'p h i l l i p i @ m i t . e d u')
faculty.email_angle: 'Separating Knowledge and Perception asks what procedural data can and cannot substitute for. I hit the boundary from the other side: a diffusion encoder pretrained on unlabelled abdominal CT kept 87% of fine-tuned liver Dice when frozen, but on kidney the frozen encoder scored below random initialisation.'
faculty.notes: Currently at MIT (the OpenAI stint was a one-year visit and is described in the past tense on his own page). Caveat on fit: his lab's stated current centre of gravity is 'representational universals' and 'emergent intelligence' (artificial life, Neural MMO, LLM-driven program evolution) - label efficiency and medical imaging are not group topics. Rated Partial for that reason. Contact policy could not be verified either way; treat any email as unprompted.

faculty.rank: Associate Professor; Germeshausen Career Development Professor
faculty.department: MIT EECS and Institute for Medical Engineering & Science (IMES); affiliations with Jameel Clinic, LIDS, IDSS, CSAIL
faculty.research_areas: Machine learning for health that is robust, private and fair; uncertainty quantification; whether benchmarks actually predict deployment behaviour; clinical ML evaluation methodology.
faculty.why_match: On SPIDER, Akshat swept confidence thresholding against Monte-Carlo-dropout uncertainty as pseudo-label filters and found that COMBINING them adds nothing (MCDO 0.7910-0.7922, comparable to thresholding alone) - a negative result about redundancy between two uncertainty signals. Ghassemi's 'Complementing Self-Consistency with Cross-Model Disagreement for Uncertainty Quantification' (ICLR 2026) is the same question one level up: when do two different uncertainty signals actually carry independent information? And her position paper 'Benchmarks Do Not Measure Deployment Readiness in Clinical AI' (ICML 2026) is the argument Akshat's own polyp analysis supports from the inside - his headline three-class Dice of 0.9525 is not comparable to binary polyp-only baselines, and the recoverable polyp-only Dice (~0.873) sits below three of four comparators.
faculty.key_paper_1: Position: Benchmarks Do Not Measure Deployment Readiness in Clinical AI. H. Zhang, H. Jeong, O. Salaudeen, W. Gerych, N. Shah, M. Ghassemi. ICML 2026.
faculty.key_paper_2: Complementing Self-Consistency with Cross-Model Disagreement for Uncertainty Quantification. K. Hamidieh, V. Thost, W. Gerych, M. Yurochkin, M. Ghassemi. ICLR 2026.
faculty.scholar: not found - no Google Scholar link is provided on healthyml.org or her MIT bio page; do not guess a profile ID.
faculty.taking_students: Yes, via multiple pools. Lab page: 'Dr. Ghassemi admits PhD students from the MIT EECS, IDSS, and HST pools.'
faculty.contact_policy: VERBATIM from https://healthyml.org/ ('Joining the Lab'): 'If you are interested in doing a PhD with the Healthy ML group, Dr. Ghassemi admits PhD students from the MIT EECS, IDSS, and HST pools. Please plan to apply to any or all of these programs, and indicate in your application that you would be interested in working with her. Unfortunately, MIT does not allow for direct admission from an individual PI to the institution.' For UROP/MEng: 'talk to a graduate student or postdoc who might be closest to your research interest.' No invitation to email her directly about PhD admission.
faculty.email_angle: Better route: approach a Healthy ML PhD student, per the lab's own advice. Essay hook: 'Your position paper argues benchmarks do not measure deployment readiness; my own polyp result is a small case study - a three-class Dice of 0.9525 that is not comparable to the binary polyp-only baselines it was ranked against.'

The overlap is uncertainty/evaluation methodology plus the health domain. She is also the widest door: EECS, IDSS and HST pools all reach her.

faculty.rank: Thomas Siebel Professor of EECS and IDSS
faculty.department: MIT EECS / Institute for Data, Systems, and Society
faculty.research_areas: Diffusion and flow-matching generative models, generator matching, flow-map distillation, discrete diffusion; representation guidance for diffusion training; conformal prediction and calibrated selective classification; structured/semi-structured data (molecules, proteins, text).
faculty.why_match: Two of Akshat's threads land inside this group. (1) His DDPM-pretrain-then-transfer experiment on BTCV asks whether the denoising objective builds a representation worth keeping - Jaakkola's 'Learning Diffusion Models with Flexible Representation Guidance' (NeurIPS 2025) is a direct treatment of coupling representation learning to the diffusion objective. (2) A-PDF's rejection of the discriminator score in favour of an explicit distributional test (Mahalanobis/kNN against the class-proportion distribution of 447 real masks) is, in effect, a hand-built conformal-style acceptance rule; Jaakkola's 'Conformal Prediction Sets with Limited False Positives' (ICML 2022) and 'Calibrated Selective Classification' (TMLR 2022) are the principled version. His 'Flow Map Distillation Without Data' (CVPR 2026) also covers Akshat's secondary interest F (one-step generative models).
faculty.key_paper_1: Learning Diffusion Models with Flexible Representation Guidance. C. Wang, C. Zhou, S. Gupta, Z. Lin, S. Jegelka, S. Bates, T. Jaakkola. NeurIPS 2025.
faculty.key_paper_2: Flow Map Distillation Without Data. S. Tong, N. Ma, S. Xie, T. Jaakkola. CVPR 2026.
faculty.taking_students: Unstated on his site. Group is very active (multiple ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS 2026 papers listed) and he co-advises heavily - his people list marks most current students '(c) = co-advised'.
faculty.contact_policy: not stated - no prospective-student or emailing instruction appears on people.csail.mit.edu/tommi as of 2026-08-28.

faculty.department: MIT EECS; LIDS; Statistics and Data Science Center; IDSS
faculty.research_areas: Quantifying uncertainty and robustness in data analysis; how much a conclusion depends on a small subset of the data (approximate cross-validation, infinitesimal jackknife, worst-case data dropping); Bayesian nonparametrics; spatial uncertainty quantification.
faculty.why_match: Akshat's SPIDER study contains a data-valuation result he did not frame as one: the per-class confidence thresholds calibrated on 5 reference images match those calibrated on 304, meaning the entire filtering decision is driven by a handful of examples. Broderick's 'An automatic finite-sample robustness metric: when can dropping a little data change conclusions?' (Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A, 2026, Parts I and II) is the formal machinery for exactly that question, and 'Dropping Just a Handful of Preferences Can Change Top Large Language Model Rankings' (ICLR 2026) shows the same phenomenon flipping published leaderboards - which is the mirror image of Akshat's polyp finding that his winning margin (0.0049 Dice) is smaller than plausible seed noise.
faculty.key_paper_1: An automatic finite-sample robustness metric: when can dropping a little data change conclusions? Part I: definitions and experiments. R. Giordano*, R. Meager*, T. Broderick. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A, 2026.
faculty.key_paper_2: Dropping Just a Handful of Preferences Can Change Top Large Language Model Rankings. J.Y. Huang*, Y. Shen*, D. Wei, T. Broderick. ICLR 2026.
faculty.taking_students: Yes. Homepage section 'Interested in working with me?' gives an active route and she lists five current PhD students/postdocs.
faculty.contact_policy: VERBATIM: 'To apply to work with me as a PhD student, submit your application to MIT EECS; more info at this link. I can also advise PhD students accepted to other appropriate programs at MIT; e.g., I have advised PhDs in Math, CSB, and SES.' No prohibition on email is stated, but no invitation either.
faculty.email_angle: 'Your automatic robustness metric asks when dropping a little data changes the conclusion. My pseudo-label filtering thresholds calibrated on 5 reference images matched those from 304 - I read that as calibration efficiency at the time, but it is really a statement that the whole decision rests on a handful of points.'
faculty.notes: Currently at MIT. Rated Partial - this is a statistics/uncertainty group, not a deep-learning or vision group, so Akshat would be changing methodological register substantially. Included because interest D (data valuation / dataset quality) has no better-matched MIT home, and because her rigour-first style is the closest match to his stated method identity of anyone in this file.

faculty.research_areas: Efficient AI: model compression, pruning, quantization (Deep Compression, AWQ, SmoothQuant), TinyML and on-device inference, hardware-aware NAS, sparse attention, efficient diffusion and one-step distilled generative models (SANA, SANA-Sprint), multi-sensor fusion for autonomous driving.
faculty.why_match: This is the only MIT lab that matches Akshat's engineering track directly. As Perception Lead on a 16-person autonomous go-kart team he built a ROS 2 LiDAR-camera fusion stack running segmentation at 56 FPS; Han's 'BEVFusion: Multi-Task Multi-Sensor Fusion with Unified Bird's-Eye View Representation' (ICRA 2023) is the canonical version of that architecture, and its central contribution is a latency fix ('optimized BEV pooling, reducing latency by more than 40x') of exactly the kind Akshat had to improvise. On the research side, his AWQ line (MLSys 2024 Best Paper) plus the SANA-Sprint one-step distillation work cover interest F, and connect to his co-founded MedTech startup's parallel GPU inference stack.
faculty.key_paper_1: BEVFusion: Multi-Task Multi-Sensor Fusion with Unified Bird's-Eye View Representation. Z. Liu*, H. Tang*, A. Amini, X. Yang, H. Mao, D.L. Rus, S. Han. IEEE ICRA 2023.
faculty.key_paper_2: AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration. MLSys 2024 (Best Paper Award).
faculty.taking_students: Unstated - no admissions statement found on hanlab.mit.edu as of 2026-08-28. Group is extremely active (ICLR 2026 orals, CVPR 2026, IROS 2026).
faculty.contact_policy: not stated - no prospective-student instruction or email policy found on hanlab.mit.edu/songhan or the HAN Lab site as of 2026-08-28.
faculty.email_angle: 'BEVFusion's 40x BEV-pooling speedup is the fix I did not have: on our autonomous go-kart I got LiDAR-camera fused segmentation to 56 FPS by cutting model capacity rather than by fixing the view-transform bottleneck.'
faculty.notes: Currently at MIT. Rated Partial and listed last on purpose: this matches Akshat's SECONDARY interests (F and G) and his engineering record, not his ranked interests A-E. The lab's current output is almost entirely LLM/VLM/video-generation efficiency systems work - if he names Han he should be honest that it is an efficiency-and-systems pitch, not a label-efficiency one. Much of the lab's recent work is co-branded with NVIDIA (NVlabs repos), which is worth knowing about IP and publication norms.
